conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Mr. Johnson, I’m Dr. Patel. You’re in the ICU. You were brought in after having trouble breathing and passing out. You’re on a breathing machine now to help you rest.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I… I remember coughing a lot. My wife called help. Am I going to be okay?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re doing everything we can. Your lungs are very inflamed, and we’re treating it like a severe pneumonia. We’ve started antibiotics and are checking for infections.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We did a bronchoscopy yesterday. We took samples from your lungs to check for infections. So far, we haven’t found a clear cause.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No infection? Then what’s causing this?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re considering other causes. One possibility is a condition called BOOP—organizing pneumonia. It’s inflammation, not infection. It can happen after transplants.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your kidney function is a concern. Your creatinine went up, likely due to cyclosporine. We’ve reduced the dose and are watching closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I was on cyclosporine for GVHD prevention. Is it hurting my kidneys?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it can. We’re tapering it off and will switch you to tacrolimus soon. Your kidneys should improve as we reduce it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re still concerned about your lungs. The chest X-ray shows persistent opacities. We’re continuing antibiotics but watching for other causes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your breathing is still labored. We’re increasing oxygen support. We’re also giving diuretics to reduce fluid in your lungs.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We did an ultrasound of your legs—no blood clots. That’s good. We’re ruling out other causes of your breathing issues.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your fever has persisted. We’re checking your sinuses. A CT showed some fluid in the sphenoid sinus. ENT is involved.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Could that be causing the fever?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly, but the aspirate came back negative. We think the fever may be from inflammation, not infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We did another bronchoscopy. The results still show no infection. We’re leaning toward BOOP as the main cause.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So no infection at all?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No bacteria, virus, or fungus found. All tests are negative. We’re stopping most antibiotics and starting high-dose steroids for BOOP.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re on methylprednisolone now. It’s a strong anti-inflammatory. We’ll taper it slowly over weeks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your oxygen levels are slowly improving. The steroids seem to be helping. We’re hopeful.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re seeing improvement on the chest X-ray. The lung opacities are clearing. This supports the BOOP diagnosis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel a little stronger. When can I get off the ventilator?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re preparing to wean you. Your lungs are healing. We’ll start trials off the vent soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great news—you tolerated a spontaneous breathing trial well. We’ll extubate you today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I’m ready to breathe on my own.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re off the vent and on oxygen. Your breathing is stable. We’ll keep you on 6 liters for now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You had a brief desaturation yesterday. We gave extra diuresis. Your weight is down, and breathing improved.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I get short of breath when I move. Is that normal?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, after being on a vent and being ill, your muscles are weak. Physical therapy will help rebuild strength.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We did a CT chest. It shows improvement in lung inflammation. The left pleural effusion is gone.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your blood sugars are high. Steroids can cause this. We’re starting insulin to manage it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I don’t have diabetes. Will this go away?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Likely yes. Once we taper the steroids, your sugars should normalize. We’ll monitor closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You had chest pain with deep breaths. We did a stress test—no heart ischemia. Your ejection fraction is mildly reduced at 49%.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is my heart damaged?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not severely. It’s mild systolic dysfunction. We’ll manage it with meds and follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You developed facial numbness a few days ago. MRI and MRA were normal. Likely due to low blood pressure at the time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It scared me. Is it gone for good?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, and it hasn’t returned. We adjusted your blood pressure meds to prevent recurrence.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your mycophenolate dose is being tapered. Your oncologist will adjust it further at follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re making steady progress. Oxygen requirement is down to 2 liters. We’re planning for transfer to the floor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We found Enterococcus in your urine, but it’s likely contamination. No treatment needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your pressure ulcers on the buttocks are healing. Keep using the barrier cream as instructed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re down to 1 liter of oxygen. Lungs are much clearer. We’re switching to oral prednisone.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: How long do I need to take the steroids?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: For several weeks. You’ll follow up with pulmonology. They’ll guide the taper based on your CT and breathing tests.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your kidney function has stabilized. Creatinine is down to 0.9. That’s a good sign.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re planning discharge. You’ll go to pulmonary rehab to continue recovery.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m ready to go. What meds will I be on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Prednisone twice daily, mycophenolate twice daily, voriconazole, atovaquone, metoprolol, and aspirin every other day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your repeat CT shows continued improvement. The lung inflammation is resolving well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re breathing comfortably on room air. We’ll discharge you soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Final plan: Discharge tomorrow. Continue all meds. Follow up with pulmonology, oncology, and cardiology.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you for everything. I feel lucky to be here.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve worked hard. Keep up with rehab and monitoring. Call if you have fever, chest pain, or trouble breathing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. I’m grateful for your care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re cleared for discharge. The transport team will take you to the rehab facility.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m ready. Thank you, Doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just checking in. How’s rehab going?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It’s tough, but I’m improving. Breathing better every day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good to hear. Keep it up. See you in clinic next week.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your outpatient labs are stable. Continue the current plan.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One last call before your follow-up. Any new symptoms?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, just tired. But I’m walking more each day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s expected. Recovery takes time. You’re doing great.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your pulmonologist confirmed improvement. They’ll continue guiding your steroid taper.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m so relieved. Thank you for getting me through this.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You did the hard work. We’re just glad you’re on the mend.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Final update: All your follow-ups are scheduled. Keep taking your meds and attending rehab.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. I appreciate all your support.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: This is your last day of our care. You’ve made an amazing recovery. Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor. I’ll never forget your help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Stay strong and keep improving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Goodbye.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Goodbye, Mr. Johnson. Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just confirming your discharge instructions one last time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I have my meds, follow-ups, and rehab schedule.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. Call if anything changes. We’re here if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Transport is here. Safe travels to rehab.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you again. I’m ready for the next step.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve come a long way. Keep up the good work.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Goodbye.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Goodbye. Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Final note: Patient discharged in stable condition, breathing comfortably on room air.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Care team, thank you for your excellent work on this complex case.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello Mr. Johnson, I'm Dr. Patel. I understand you came in with pain and a rash on your right leg?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, doctor. It started last night—sudden pain, no injury. This morning, I saw the red rash, like a sunburn, and couldn’t walk on it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. You were given antibiotics in the clinic—vancomycin and cefepime—because we’re concerned about infection, especially given your transplant history.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Right, I’m on a lot of meds already. Is this cellulitis? Could it be something else?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s likely. The rash is warm, tender, and spreading—classic signs. But we’ll rule out deeper issues. We’ve ordered blood cultures and an X-ray of your leg.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my blood pressure was low earlier. Should I be worried?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It was 105 over 58. You recently started carvedilol—could be contributing. We’ll monitor it. Not septic yet, but we’re cautious.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And my platelets are low again—53. Is that from the transplant?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, thrombocytopenia is common post-transplant. We’ll keep an eye on it, but no transfusion needed now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks. My vision’s been blurry too—worse in the mornings. Should I mention that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, absolutely. You’ve been on long-term steroids—could be early cataracts. We’ll arrange an ophthalmology consult.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your X-ray shows no bone infection or fracture. Ultrasound ruled out a blood clot in your leg.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So not osteomyelitis or DVT. That’s a relief.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Correct. The rash is likely cellulitis. Blood cultures are still pending, but no growth so far.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Could it be fungal? I’m on voriconazole for aspergillosis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We considered that, but the rapid response to antibiotics makes bacterial cause more likely. We’ll continue current treatment.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my kidneys? My last creatinine was up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, mild acute kidney injury. Ultrasound shows no blockage. Likely from dehydration or medication. We’re holding lisinopril for now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had chronic kidney disease for years. Is this worse?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not significantly. We’ll monitor and adjust meds. Your blood pressure should stabilize as you improve.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—both blood cultures came back negative. No bacteria grew. That supports our current plan.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So no bacteremia? But I had a fever initially.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You did, but sometimes immunocompromised patients have atypical presentations. The antibiotics are working—the rash is improving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my heart? I saw an echo was done.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your ejection fraction is stable, but there’s new mild pulmonary hypertension. We’ll follow that with cardiology.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had heart issues since chemo. Is this related?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly. Post-chemo cardiomyopathy can evolve. We’ll keep monitoring, but no immediate changes to your meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your rash is much better—smaller, less red. We’re switching from IV antibiotics to oral clindamycin and ciprofloxacin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great. How long do I need to take them?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: For 14 days, finishing one week after your podiatry appointment. They didn’t think your toe redness was the source.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh right, I have that scheduled. My toes have been sore for months—neuropathy?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Likely. You have peripheral neuropathy from past treatments. We’ll keep you on gabapentin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my prednisone dose was increased. Why?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: To help with inflammation from the infection and your underlying sarcoidosis. But we’re watching your blood sugar closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m on insulin now. Is that permanent?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not necessarily. Steroids raise blood sugar. We’ll taper the prednisone and adjust insulin as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. Vital signs are stable, rash is nearly gone. We’re planning discharge tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. What about my meds at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll continue all your transplant meds—mycophenolate, voriconazole, acyclovir, atovaquone. Plus the new antibiotics for two weeks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the insulin?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, glargine daily and aspart with meals based on your sugar. We’ll reassess after the prednisone taper.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Should I restart my blood pressure meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Carvedilol is restarted. Hold lisinopril for now—your kidneys are recovering. We’ll recheck labs next week.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the ophthalmology appointment?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Scheduled for next week. Blurry vision has improved, so likely steroid-related changes, not infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You’re cleared for discharge. Your vitals are normal, and the rash is minimal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What signs should I watch for?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Fever, increasing redness or swelling, or shortness of breath. Otherwise, follow up with your team and finish all antibiotics.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my AML? Still in remission?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, no signs of relapse. Continue all transplant-related meds and monitoring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks, doctor. I feel much better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care, and call if anything changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will do.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Nurse will go over your discharge instructions and medications now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You're welcome. Get some rest at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: And keep your leg elevated when possible to reduce swelling.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll see you in follow-up soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Appreciate it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care, Mr. Johnson.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: You too, doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Have a safe trip home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Call us with any concerns.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Mr. Johnson, I’m Dr. Patel. You’ve been admitted because of fevers and rigors this morning. Can you tell me what happened?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I woke up with chills and shaking, like full-body rigors. I had a fever at clinic—over 101—and my heart was racing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. Your blood pressure dropped when you arrived, and your oxygen was low—85% on 2 liters. We started antibiotics and moved you to the ICU for monitoring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It scared me. I couldn’t catch my breath. I felt like I was drowning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s what we call hypoxic respiratory failure. You responded well to oxygen on a face mask. We’re treating you for sepsis, likely from an infection in your central line.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My old Hickman line? But it’s been fine.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We drew blood cultures. If they grow bacteria, it’ll confirm the source. For now, you’re on vancomycin and meropenem—broad coverage until we know more.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. My back pain got worse this morning too. Is that related?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We ordered a CT of your spine to check for infection like discitis. But so far, no signs of osteomyelitis. Likely musculoskeletal, given your history.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your blood cultures came back positive for a bacteria called Stenotrophomonas maltophilia.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Steno-what? Is that serious?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s a rare bacterium, often linked to central lines in immunocompromised patients. It’s treatable, but we need to remove your Hickman line to stop the source.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So the line has to come out?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. We’ll place a new one later if needed. We’re switching your antibiotics to IV Bactrim, which works well against this bug.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve taken Bactrim before. I hope my kidneys handle it this time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re watching your creatinine. It’s already rising a bit. Bactrim can make creatinine look high without actual kidney damage. We’ll monitor closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your chest CT shows new nodules in your right upper lobe. They suggest infection spreading through the airways.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is it pneumonia? Could it be fungal?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly. But your galactomannan and beta-glucan tests were negative, so aspergillus is less likely. We’re continuing voriconazole as a precaution.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my breathing? It’s still labored.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your oxygen needs have improved—from 5 liters to 3. We think it’s partly from the infection, but you have underlying lung disease from BOOP.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Last night, you had a code blue—acute respiratory distress after your line was flushed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I remember feeling like I couldn’t breathe. Then I got foggy. I was scared.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You desaturated to 69%, but bagging helped. No intubation was needed. It may have been a reaction to line debris or a small air embolus.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Could it happen again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Unlikely now that the line is out. We’ll keep you on close monitoring. Your oxygen has been stable since.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your repeat blood cultures are negative. That’s a good sign—your antibiotics are working.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. But I’ve been forgetting things. I lost track of what the nurse said yesterday.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We noticed. It could be from the sepsis or low oxygen. We ordered a brain MRI to rule out stroke or injury.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your MRI came back. No stroke or brain injury. Just mild atrophy, which is common with age. Your confusion should improve.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I was worried it was permanent.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s not. We’ll keep an eye on it. Your heart function is another concern—your echo showed an ejection fraction of 40%.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s lower than before. Is my heart failing?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s systolic dysfunction, possibly from sepsis or prior chemo. No fluid overload now, so we’re holding lasix. We’ll follow up in heart failure clinic.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your kidney function is plateauing. Creatinine is 2.1, but urine tests show no damage. We think it’s Bactrim affecting the lab value.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it might not be real kidney injury?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. We stopped Bactrim yesterday. If it’s just a lab effect, your creatinine should drop in a few days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your creatinine is down to 1.8 today. That supports our theory. We’ll keep monitoring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. But now my right big toe is red and throbbing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Looks like an infected ingrown toenail. We’ll start vancomycin and get podiatry to evaluate.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Podiatry saw you. They recommend a wedge resection to remove the ingrown portion.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had this problem for years. I missed my appointment because I was here.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll schedule it soon. In the meantime, we’re adding augmentin after the procedure for coverage.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The procedure went well. They removed the nail wedge and sent cultures. You’re on a 5-day course of augmentin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It already feels better. When can I walk on it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Keep it elevated and limit weight-bearing for a few days. Podiatry will see you after discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your chest X-ray today shows significant improvement. The infiltrates are nearly gone.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel less short of breath too. Can I go home soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re getting there. Your oxygen is at 1.5 liters at rest—close to your baseline. We’ll wean further.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your creatinine is now 1.6—back to baseline. That confirms it was the Bactrim effect.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great. What about my heart? Will the EF recover?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly. Sepsis can depress heart function temporarily. We’ll repeat the echo in clinic.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your wound culture from the toe grew Staph aureus, but it’s sensitive to the augmentin. No change in antibiotics needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. My vision’s been blurry too. Is that from steroids?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Likely. You’ve been on prednisone long-term. We’ve scheduled ophthalmology to check for cataracts or glaucoma.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve been off IV antibiotics for two days with no fever. That’s excellent progress.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel much stronger. When do I get discharged?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: If you keep improving, likely in 2–3 days. We’ll finalize your discharge plan tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: All set. You’re stable, afebrile, and on oral meds. We’re planning discharge tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. What follow-ups do I need?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Kidney clinic for creatinine, heart failure clinic for your echo, pulmonary for the nodules, podiatry for your toe, and ophthalmology for your eyes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my AML? Is it still in remission?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. Daily blood counts show no blasts. You’re still on mycophenolate for graft protection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I stopped atovaquone. Should I restart PCP prophylaxis?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. We’re switching you back to Bactrim at a lower dose for prevention. We’ll add it to your discharge meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Last day in the hospital. You’re on 1.5 liters oxygen at rest, 3 with activity—back to baseline.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m ready to go home. Thank you for everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You did well. Continue all meds, finish the augmentin, and watch for fever, toe redness, or breathing trouble.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. And I’ll make all my follow-up appointments.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. We’ll see you in clinic soon. Take care, Mr. Johnson.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just confirming—you’re discharged as of today. Your condition is stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I’m packed and ready. I feel so much better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Excellent. Remember to follow up on all your appointments and call if anything changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take it easy, and we’ll see you soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Drive safe.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. Have a good recovery at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I plan to.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll be in touch with your primary team to coordinate care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s reassuring. I appreciate it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Our goal is to keep you healthy. Don’t hesitate to call with concerns.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I won’t. Thanks again for all your help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re very welcome. Take care, Mr. Johnson.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: You too. See you in clinic.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Absolutely. Stay well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello Mr. Johnson, I'm Dr. Patel. I understand you've been having a lot of joint pain and toe pain. Can you tell me more about what’s been going on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, doctor. The joint pain is everywhere—shoulders, hips, knees, elbows. It’s worse than it’s ever been. And my big toes are red, swollen, and bleeding. It’s been like this since my last hospital stay.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. And you mentioned it improves a bit with oxycodone but gets worse with activity. Any fevers recently?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I had a low-grade fever two days ago—100.3—but it went away on its own. No chest pain or trouble breathing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Given your history with AML and transplant, we need to be careful. We’ll run some blood tests and check for infection. We also need to look at your toes more closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been on Augmentin since the last discharge. Is that still okay?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re going to stop the Augmentin. Your wound culture showed MRSA, so we’ll start IV vancomycin instead to make sure we’re covering the right bacteria.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: MRSA? I thought it was just a regular staph infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It was coagulase-positive staph before, but now it’s confirmed as MRSA. That means we need stronger antibiotics. Vancomycin is the best choice for that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. What about my joint pain? It’s exhausting.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re checking your blood cultures now. No growth so far. But given your history, we’re also concerned about graft-versus-host disease, or GVHD, which can cause muscle and joint pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: GVHD? I thought that was mostly skin or gut.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It can affect joints and muscles too. We’re also ruling out other things like gout or avascular necrosis from long-term steroid use. We’ve ordered hip X-rays for that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And my potassium was high last time. Is that still an issue?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your potassium was 4.2 today—borderline. We gave you Kayexalate to bring it down safely. We’ll keep monitoring it, especially since your kidneys are still recovering.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My creatinine is still high, isn’t it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’s 1.5, better than last time but still elevated. We think it’s from the Bactrim you were on. We’ve stopped that and are giving fluids to help your kidneys.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m also on voriconazole for aspergillosis. Should I keep that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, absolutely. We’ll continue that as scheduled. It’s important for your lung health.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your hip X-rays came back—no signs of avascular necrosis or fractures. That’s reassuring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. So what’s causing the pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re leaning toward GVHD. Your pain is widespread, and you’ve responded partially to steroids in the past. We’re going to increase your prednisone dose to see if that helps.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been on prednisone before. Won’t that raise my blood sugar?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It might. We’ll monitor your glucose closely and adjust your insulin. You’re on Lantus and sliding scale aspart—correct?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes. I’ve noticed my sugars running higher since the last hospital stay.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s likely from the steroids. We’ll keep checking four times a day and adjust as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We also did an ultrasound on your left arm because of the swelling. No blood clot—good news.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the old catheter site? It still hurts.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The ultrasound showed a small collection there, likely a hematoma from the removal. No abscess, so we don’t need to drain it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your joint pain seems a bit better today. How are you feeling?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Actually, much better. The increased prednisone really helped. I can move without wincing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. It supports our thought that this is GVHD-related. We’ll keep you on the higher dose for now and taper slowly as an outpatient.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about my toe? It still looks bad.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Podiatry is coming to see you. They may need to do a small procedure to clean it out.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The podiatry team did an excisional debridement of your left big toe. They removed the infected tissue. You’ll stay on vancomycin to make sure it clears up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I need more surgery?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not right now. This should help it heal. We’ll keep the area clean and monitor for infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We got the X-ray of your toes. No signs of osteomyelitis—no bone infection. That’s excellent.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s just the skin and nail?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. The MRSA is in the soft tissue, not the bone. That means antibiotics and wound care should be enough.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been on IV vancomycin. Will I need to keep that at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. We’re going to place a PICC line tomorrow so you can finish a 10-day course at home. It’s safer and more effective than oral antibiotics for MRSA.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that the line in the arm?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. It goes into a vein in your arm and leads to a large vein near your heart. You’ll get nursing support at home to manage it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—your joint pain is gone, your toe is healing, and your labs are stable. We’re planning to discharge you today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. What do I need to do at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Stop the Augmentin. Keep taking vancomycin through the PICC line for 10 more days. Take acyclovir twice a day and Bactrim three times a week for prevention.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the prednisone?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll take 20mg in the morning and 15mg at night for three more nights, then your doctor will help taper it down slowly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: When do I follow up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: See your transplant team in one week. Also follow up with podiatry. Call us if you develop fever, increased pain, or pus from the toe.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The PICC line was placed successfully in your right arm. It’s working well, and you’re ready to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, doctor. I feel so much better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Keep up with the meds, rest, and we’ll see how you do. Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Nurse will go over your discharge instructions one more time before you leave.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, sounds good.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: And remember—no heavy lifting with that arm until the PICC is out.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. I’ll be careful.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve done well. We’re glad we could help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Appreciate it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care, Mr. Johnson.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: You too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll see you in follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I’ll be there.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Have a safe trip home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello Mr. Johnson, I'm Dr. Patel. I understand you've been feeling unwell since this morning. Can you tell me what’s been going on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I woke up with nausea and threw up—dark brown stuff. I also had a fever, around 101. I didn’t have any diarrhea or belly pain, though.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. And you mentioned joint pain making it hard to walk. Has that been worse lately?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It’s been bad, but I’ve had it for months since the transplant. I’ve been on prednisone for it. But today, the nausea and fever came out of nowhere.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You got your Rituxan infusion yesterday, correct? That could sometimes cause a reaction, but we need to rule out infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I had it yesterday. Could that be why I feel so sick?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s possible, but your fever and the brown vomit are concerning. We’ve started you on IV antibiotics—cefepime and vancomycin—just in case it’s an infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Is my lung okay? I’ve had breathing issues before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your initial chest X-ray was clear, but we’re doing a CT scan to look more closely. Your oxygen level was in the 80s on room air, so we’ve given you oxygen through a nasal cannula.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. I do feel better with the oxygen.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Mr. Johnson, the CT scan of your chest shows small nodules in both upper lobes. They weren’t there before. This suggests an infection in the airways, possibly from an atypical bacteria.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is it pneumonia? I’ve had that before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it looks like pneumonia. We don’t see any viruses in your nasal swab, and your blood cultures haven’t grown anything yet. So we’re treating it as bacterial.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will the antibiotics I’m on now be enough?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: For now, yes. We’re using broad-spectrum antibiotics to cover all possibilities. Once we know more, we might adjust.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your respiratory virus test came back negative—no flu, RSV, or others. Blood tests also show no CMV or fungal infections.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not a virus?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, it doesn’t look like it. The pattern on your CT scan still points to a bacterial infection, possibly atypical. We’ll keep you on the current antibiotics today and reassess.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My nausea is better. I haven’t vomited since yesterday.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s great to hear. It might have been related to the infection or even the Rituxan. Since you’re improving, we’re confident we’re on the right track.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your temperature has been normal since yesterday. That’s a good sign the antibiotics are working.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel stronger too. Do I still need the IV antibiotics?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re going to switch you to an oral antibiotic called levofloxacin. It covers the kind of bacteria we suspect. You’ll take it for 14 days at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that safe with my other meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ve checked. It won’t interact with your voriconazole or immunosuppressants. We’ll monitor your kidney function, though, since your creatinine is a bit high.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been on oxygen since I got here. Will I need it at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: On admission, you were in the 80s on room air. Now you’re at 95% on 2 liters. We’ll wean you down and see how you do. You may need it for ambulation for a while.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your blood cultures came back negative for bacteria, fungi, and TB. That supports our decision to treat with levofloxacin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So no dangerous bugs?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, nothing dangerous grew. That’s reassuring. Your body is likely fighting off a community-acquired pneumonia.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My joint pain is still there. Should I keep taking prednisone?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’re keeping your prednisone at 15 mg daily. It’s helping your chronic GVHD. We’ll discuss tapering with your transplant team later.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well on oral antibiotics. Your oxygen saturation is 97% on 1.5 liters. We’re planning to discharge you tomorrow if this continues.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good news. What do I need to do at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Finish the full 14-day course of levofloxacin. Keep using oxygen as needed, especially when walking. And monitor for fever, shortness of breath, or chest pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about my other meds? Anything changed?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Most are the same. We’re adding a new medication—esomeprazole—for your acid reflux. It’s called Nexium. Take it once a day as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had heartburn lately. That might help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Last night, you stayed at 96% on 1.5 liters of oxygen. You walked to the bathroom without trouble. We’re comfortable discharging you today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great. Will I need follow-up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. You’ll see your oncologist and transplant team next week. They’ll review your GVHD and medications. Also, keep your primary care visits.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m glad I’m going home. This stay was scary at first.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. But you responded well to treatment. The key is finishing the antibiotics and watching for any new symptoms.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: If I start feeling feverish again, I’ll call my doctor or come back?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Same for nausea, chest pain, or trouble breathing. Don’t hesitate to reach out.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Mr. Johnson, you’re cleared to go home. Your oxygen will be set at 2 liters for portability. Use it as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I’ll take good care of myself.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve done well. Remember: levofloxacin once daily for 14 days, Nexium for reflux, and keep all your other meds as prescribed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And I’ll follow up with my teams next week.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. Take care, Mr. Johnson. We’re glad you’re on the mend.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just a quick check before you leave. How are you feeling now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Much better. Nausea is gone, and I can walk without getting winded.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Excellent. Your oxygen sat is 98% on 1.5 liters. That’s a big improvement from when you came in.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m really grateful.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re glad we could help. Stay safe, and don’t skip those follow-ups.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: One last thing—should I avoid crowds while on antibiotics?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good question. Yes, try to avoid large gatherings and sick people. Your immune system is still recovering from the transplant and infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll stay home as much as I can.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s wise. And keep washing your hands and wearing a mask if you go out.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been taking my insulin as usual. My sugars have been okay.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. Keep monitoring. The steroids can raise your blood sugar, so your sliding scale is still important.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The home health team will set up your oxygen and check in on you. They’ll also review your meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s helpful. I was worried about managing everything alone.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re not alone. We’ve got you covered. Call us with any concerns.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor. I really appreciate it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello Mr. Johnson, I'm Dr. Patel. I understand you've been having worsening joint pain. Can you tell me more about it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, doctor. It’s been getting worse over the past two weeks. It’s in my shoulders, elbows, hips, knees, and ankles. It hurts more when I walk or go up stairs.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. Any swelling, redness, or warmth in the joints?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, not really. They don’t feel hot or swollen. But I’ve been more tired than usual and nauseous.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Any fevers or chills?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, no fevers.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I know you’ve been on OxyContin for pain. You mentioned you reduced the dose?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I cut it to once a day at night because the nausea was bad. I didn’t want to take too many painkillers either.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. But reducing the dose may have made your pain worse. We’ll work on balancing that. You also mentioned your toes hurt?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, both second toes. They’ve been sensitive, especially near the nail edge. It’s been hard to wear shoes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll have podiatry take a look. For now, we’re going to run some blood tests to check for inflammation and infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, thank you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your labs are back. Your CRP is elevated at 20.3, which suggests inflammation. But no signs of infection in your blood or urine.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not an infection?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, blood cultures and urine cultures were negative. Your symptoms are likely due to worsening graft-versus-host disease, especially since you stopped Plaquenil and changed from Tacrolimus.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I stopped Plaquenil because it made me nauseous. But I didn’t know it could affect my joints.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It can. We’ll keep you off Plaquenil but increase your prednisone from 15mg to 20mg daily to better control the inflammation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will that help with the nausea too?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly. Also, stopping Tacrolimus may have helped. We’ll also restart your OxyContin twice daily and give you morphine for breakthrough pain since oxycodone is in short supply.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m okay with that. I just want to feel better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You had a chest X-ray last night. No pneumonia or fluid. Your lungs are clear, which is good given your history.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I was worried about that after last time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Understandable. We’re also watching your blood pressure. You had a drop yesterday—felt dizzy?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, for a moment. But it passed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We think it was from the narcotic dose. We lowered it, and your pressure stabilized. No need for antibiotics.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good to know.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Morning. The vascular study on your legs was normal. Good blood flow. No blockages.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Podiatry will remove your ingrown toenails today. There was a little pus on the right side, so we’ll start a short course of Keflex.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will it hurt?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: They’ll numb your toes first. You might feel pressure, but not pain. We’ll also give you antibiotic ointment for the site.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The procedure went well. Both toenails were removed. We’ll keep the ointment on for a few days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. My joints feel a bit better already with the new dose.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. The increased prednisone and pain meds are helping. We also added Colace and senna for constipation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been bloated. Thanks for that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We also increased your esomeprazole to twice daily for your heartburn. Let us know if it persists.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had that for years. But yes, I’ll mention it if it doesn’t improve.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your kidney function is stable—creatinine around 2.0. We’ll keep monitoring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that normal for me?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’s consistent with your chronic kidney disease. No acute changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, good.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—we’re planning to discharge you today. Your pain, fatigue, and nausea have all improved.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. What changes should I expect at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll stay on 20mg prednisone daily, OxyContin twice a day, and morphine for breakthrough pain. Plaquenil is stopped, and you’ll take Keflex for three more days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the ointment?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Apply it twice a day to the right toe for four days. Also take Colace and senna as needed for constipation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. And my nausea?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re switching you to Zofran as needed. It often works better than Compazine.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll try that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Follow up with your oncologist and transplant team. Call us if you develop fever, increased pain, chest pain, or any new symptoms.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you, doctor. I feel much better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. We’ll see you in clinic soon. Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Nurse will go over your discharge instructions and medications now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’m ready.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One last thing—your graft-versus-host disease is under better control now, but long-term management will need discussion with your specialist.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I’ll bring that up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. We’re discharging you in good condition. Let’s get your paperwork started.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Appreciate all the help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. Keep up with your follow-ups.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care, Mr. Johnson.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: You too, doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll see you soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Have a safe trip home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Mr. Johnson, I'm Dr. Patel. I understand you came in from clinic today because your kidney numbers were high and you've been feeling unwell.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that’s right. My creatinine was 2.3, and I’ve been more tired than usual. I also had some trouble swallowing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. And I understand you had a brief episode when you arrived—became unresponsive for a moment. Do you remember that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Not really. I just remember lying down and then people around me. My wife said my eyes were closed and I didn’t respond.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We called a code because your potassium was high and your EKG showed peaked T waves. We gave you insulin and dextrose to bring it down quickly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, I didn’t know it was that serious. Is my potassium okay now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It was 5.5 when you arrived, which is high. We treated it, and it’s coming down. We’ll keep monitoring it. We also gave you kayexalate to help your body get rid of extra potassium.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. But why did I pass out? That’s never happened before like that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s not entirely clear. It could be related to the high potassium, or maybe a blood pressure drop. Your wife mentioned you’ve had brief episodes like this before?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, yes—maybe once or twice a week for the past few months. Just seconds, I’m told. I don’t remember them.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s important. We’ve consulted neurology. They think it’s worth checking with an EEG and maybe a Holter monitor to rule out seizures or heart rhythm issues.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: An EEG? Like for seizures? But I don’t jerk or anything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. You don’t have the typical signs, but brief lapses in awareness can still be neurological. We also noticed a tremor in your hands when you’re holding things.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that’s been there for years. Gets worse when I try to hold a cup or write. My wife calls it a shaky hand.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That sounds like an intention tremor. It’s not typical for seizures, which is reassuring. But we still want to evaluate the episodes of unresponsiveness.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can we do those tests later? I’m feeling better now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We can arrange them as outpatient tests. We’ve scheduled an EEG, a Holter monitor, carotid ultrasound, and an echocardiogram.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That sounds okay. What about my kidneys? That’s why I came in.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your baseline creatinine has been between 1.4 and 2.0. It went up to 2.3, so we’re calling this acute on chronic kidney injury. We think it’s partly due to your medications.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Like which ones?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Lisinopril, voriconazole, and Bactrim can all affect the kidneys. We’ve held your lisinopril for now because it can also raise potassium.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been on that for years. Should I stop it for good?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not necessarily. We’ll discuss restarting it with your nephrologist. We’ve also reduced your Cellcept dose because your kidney function is reduced.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And my stomach’s been bothering me—burning, especially after taking prednisone.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, prednisone can cause gastritis. You said Nexium hasn’t helped for the past three months?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, not really. I still wake up with acid.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re switching you to Protonix, which might work better. You may need prior authorization, but your oncologist can help with that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Alright. And my breathing? I’ve felt a bit swollen in the legs.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You have mild swelling, and your exam shows you’re a bit fluid overloaded. But your chest X-ray shows no pneumonia or heart failure. We’ll keep you on your furosemide.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I don’t want to end up on oxygen again like with BOOP.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re watching closely. Your heart enzymes and ABG were normal, so no sign of heart damage or breathing trouble.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning, Mr. Johnson. Your potassium is now 4.0, and creatinine is down to 1.9—back to your baseline. That’s great progress.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good to hear. No more episodes either.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: And telemetry showed no arrhythmias. The head CT was normal—no bleeding or stroke. Just some sinus inflammation, which we already knew about.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I can go home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, if you’re feeling well. We’ll discharge you tomorrow. Just need to make sure you’re stable through the night.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: All your labs are stable. You’ve had no syncopal episodes, and your vitals are good. We’re clearing you for discharge today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great. What do I need to do when I get home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Continue all your meds as listed, except hold lisinopril. Take Protonix for your stomach. And watch for fever, fainting, chest pain—come back if any of those happen.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the follow-up tests?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: All scheduled—EEG, Holter, echo, carotid ultrasound. Your oncologist and nephrologist will get the results and guide next steps.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor. I feel much better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. We’ll make sure your records are sent to your team. Take care, and see you in follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just a final check before you leave. You’re afebrile, blood pressure stable, no dizziness. You’re cleared to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Appreciate all the care. I’ll follow up on those tests right away.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. And call us if anything changes. Your wife has the discharge instructions?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, she’s got everything. Thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care, Mr. Johnson. Stay hydrated and keep up with your appointments.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Mr. Johnson, I'm Dr. Patel. I understand you had some episodes that felt like 'fits'—can you tell me what happened?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, I was at home and suddenly I couldn’t speak right. My words were jumbled. It lasted maybe two minutes, then I was okay. Happened twice this week.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Did you lose consciousness? Any shaking or weakness?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, I was awake. Just couldn’t talk. Felt scared, but no shaking.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Given your history—AML, transplant, graft-versus-host disease—we need to rule out stroke or seizure. We’ll get a CT of your head right away.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is it a stroke? I’ve been stable since the last admission.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We don’t know yet. The CT will help. You also have a fever—101. We’re concerned about infection, so we’re starting antibiotics and doing a chest X-ray.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Fever’s been on and off. Thought it was just GVHD flaring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly, but we can’t rule out pneumonia. Your chest X-ray shows some opacity in the left lower lung. We’ll monitor closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—the head CT shows no bleeding or stroke. Sinus infection is worse, but that’s not causing your speech issues.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So what’s causing the 'fits' then?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re not sure. Could be a seizure or a neurological side effect of your medications. We’re ordering an MRI and MRA of the brain tonight to look deeper.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Seizure? I’ve never had one before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s possible, especially with your medical history. We’ll also check your electrolytes and B12—deficiencies can affect the brain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your respiratory viral panel came back negative. No flu or RSV. That’s good—we can focus on other causes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So not a cold?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No. Your fever and lung findings may be from inflammation related to GVHD or infection we can’t see yet.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The MRI and MRA are back. No stroke, no tumor, no aneurysm. Your brain vessels are normal. The speech episodes aren’t from structural damage.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So what is it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We think it could be transient neurological episodes related to your transplant or medications. We’re also checking for B-complex deficiencies—low B12 can cause this.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I take supplements. Could it still be low?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, especially with GVHD affecting your gut. We’ll start B12 injections just in case.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We repeated the chest X-ray. The lung changes are stable—no new pneumonia. The opacities are likely from chronic inflammation, not infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I can stop antibiotics?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll taper them. Your fever’s gone, so likely not bacterial. We’ll keep monitoring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your labs show low B12. That could be contributing to the speech episodes. We’ll continue the injections.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will that stop the episodes?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly. We’re also considering that your steroids for GVHD might be affecting your mood and brain function. We’re calling psychiatry to help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Psychiatry? I’m not depressed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s not just depression. Steroids can cause emotional disturbances—irritability, anxiety, even transient psychosis. We want to make sure we’re covering all bases.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The psychiatrist evaluated you. They think your 'fits' may be a mix of neurological and emotional factors—what we call a predominant disturbance of emotions, possibly triggered by stress and meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not a seizure?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We can’t rule it out completely, but no EEG showed seizure activity. More likely, it’s a functional neurological episode—real symptoms, but not from structural brain damage.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will it happen again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly, but we’re adjusting your steroids and adding B12. We’ll also refer you for outpatient therapy to help manage stress.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your heart ultrasound showed mild cardiomyopathy. It’s not new, but we’ll monitor it. Also, your diabetes and cholesterol are elevated—we’ll adjust meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Diabetes? I didn’t know I had that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s secondary—likely from the steroids. We’ll start metformin and monitor your levels.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve been stable—no more episodes, fever gone, lungs clear. We’re planning discharge tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. What about the reflux? I’ve been having heartburn.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’re adding omeprazole for esophageal reflux. Steroids can worsen that too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Final chest X-ray shows improvement in the left base. No pneumonia. You’re ready for discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re discharging you today. Continue B12 injections, metformin, omeprazole, and your other meds. Follow up with hematology, neurology, and psychiatry.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And if I have another episode?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Call your doctor. If it lasts more than 5 minutes or you feel weak, go to the ER. But we think the B12 and reduced steroid dose will help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m glad it wasn’t a stroke.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, and we’ve addressed several issues—B12, mood, heart, diabetes. Keep up with follow-ups, and you should do well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Nursing will go over your discharge instructions. Any last questions?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, I think I’m good. Thanks for explaining everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care, Mr. Johnson.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Doctor, one more thing—should I avoid stress?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, as much as possible. Stress can trigger these episodes. Therapy can help you build coping strategies.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll make the appointment.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good plan. We’re here if you need us.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just confirming—you have all your prescriptions and follow-up details?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, got them. Hematology next week, then neurology.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. You’re all set.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks again, Doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care, Mr. Johnson. We’ll see you in follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Discharge paperwork is signed. You’re free to go when ready.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Appreciate all the help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Stay well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: One last thing—my wife wants to know if the 'fits' mean I can’t drive.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good question. Given the episodes involved speech, not consciousness, you may be able to drive, but check with neurology first. They’ll assess safety.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll ask them.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, better safe. Otherwise, you’re cleared.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks, Doctor. Really appreciate it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care, Mr. Johnson. We’re here if anything comes up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will do.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re officially discharged. Have a safe trip home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello Mr. Johnson, I'm Dr. Patel. I'll be your doctor during this stay. I understand you've been having a cough for about a week?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
