conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’s been constant. Not too bad, but won’t go away. It’s productive—clear mucus. I’ve been more tired than usual.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Any fever, chills, or shortness of breath?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No fever. My oxygen at home is still around 95% on 2 liters when I walk. But I’ve started using it at rest just to feel better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I see your son has been coughing too. That’s helpful. We’ll check your lungs and get a chest X-ray to start.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your chest X-ray came back—no pneumonia or fluid. Lungs look clear. But we’re going to do a CT scan tomorrow to get a closer look, given your history.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Because of the transplant and GVHD?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. You’ve had lung issues before—BOOP and chronic GVHD. We need to tell if this is infection, a flare, or something else.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Makes sense. I’ve been on Symbicort and Singulair at home. Should I keep using them?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ll continue both. We also gave you azithromycin in the ER as a precaution. We’ll see what the CT shows tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your labs are stable—white count is normal, kidney function slightly elevated but consistent with baseline.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Any sign of infection?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Blood cultures are negative so far. Viral panel came back—no flu, RSV, or other common viruses.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So not viral?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not the common ones. But your son had similar symptoms, so we still think it could be a mild viral upper respiratory infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The CT scan is back. There’s new thickening in the airway walls and mucus plugging, especially in the lower lobes. Some new hazy spots in the right upper lobe.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is it GVHD?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The radiologist thinks it’s more likely infection. There’s no significant air trapping, which we’d expect with GVHD. So we’re leaning toward bacterial or viral bronchitis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Should we do a bronchoscopy?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We consulted pulmonary. They don’t think it’s necessary right now. Your oxygen is stable, and you’re not severely ill. We’ll treat empirically.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What does that mean?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll start you on levofloxacin—an antibiotic—to cover possible bacterial infection. We’ll also continue your usual prednisone dose, not increase it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I was worried they’d bump up the steroids again. I don’t handle them well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re avoiding that. Your diabetes is well-controlled, and we don’t want to worsen side effects. You’re on the lowest effective dose.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your CMV test came back—no virus detected. Urine culture is clean. Sputum sample was too contaminated to read, so we won’t repeat it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So still no bug identified?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, but that’s common. The CT findings and your exposure at home point to infection. We’re doing the right thing with the antibiotic.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I also got IVIG yesterday. Why was that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve been getting IVIG regularly through your oncologist. It helps with immune support, especially with chronic GVHD. We continued it as scheduled.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Ah, right. I forgot it was due.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your oxygen levels are steady. You walked to the nurses’ station today—sats stayed at 94%. That’s good progress.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I still cough, but less than when I came in.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s expected. The inflammation takes time to settle. We’ll keep the levofloxacin for a full course.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Any other new meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We started allopurinol. Your uric acid was high. It’s to prevent gout flares, especially with your kidney function.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had gout before. That makes sense.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. Another chest X-ray shows the right upper lobe opacity is still there, but no worsening. We think it’s resolving slowly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I can go home soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, likely tomorrow. We’ll discharge you on oral levofloxacin for a few more days and continue all your home meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the oxygen?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Same as before—use it with exertion. Check your sats a few times a day. Call your doctor if they drop below 92% or you feel more short of breath.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Any follow-up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. You have oncology follow-up scheduled. And we’re setting you up with a new primary care doctor next week.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I’ve been bouncing between specialists.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Morning! Today’s the day. You’re cleared to go home. Your cough is improving, oxygen is stable, and no signs of infection worsening.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great. What about the new meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Levofloxacin—take one pill every 48 hours for five doses. Allopurinol—once daily. Discuss both with your PCP at your follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my usual meds—anything changed?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No changes. Keep taking Symbicort, CellCept, prednisone, and everything else as prescribed. Don’t skip the inhaler this time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll try not to. Thanks for explaining everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Call us if the cough worsens, fever develops, or oxygen drops. Otherwise, rest and take it easy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will do. Appreciate the care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care, Mr. Johnson. We’ll see you in follow-up if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: One more thing—should I worry about the lung changes long-term?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The changes were acute and likely infectious. With treatment, they should resolve. Your last echo showed improved heart function, which helps your lungs too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s reassuring. My exercise tolerance has been poor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Partly due to deconditioning. As you heal, slowly increase activity. Talk to your pulmonologist about pulmonary rehab if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll bring it up. Thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. Just keep up with your care team.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Have a good day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You too. Safe travels home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: One last question—can I see my CT images?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you can request them through medical records. The key point is the changes looked infectious, not a GVHD flare.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. I was worried.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Totally understandable. But all signs point to recovery. Keep your appointments and stay on your meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks for your patience.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Of course. Take care, Mr. Johnson.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Mr. Johnson, I'm Dr. Patel. I understand you've been feeling unwell since this morning—fevers, chills, and some nausea?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that’s right. I had a fever last night, maybe up to 102, and I just couldn’t get out of bed. My wife brought me to clinic in the wheelchair.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. And you mentioned a cough and one episode of diarrhea this morning?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Just a little cough, no sputum. The diarrhea was very small—more like a slip-up. I’m usually constipated, so it surprised me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Got it. And how’s your breathing? You came in on oxygen—has that been more than usual?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, I used it because I felt weak, but I’m not short of breath. My usual oxygen is just a few hours a day when I’m tired.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. We’ve checked your vitals—you’re not running a fever now—and we’ve ordered blood work, a chest X-ray, and some cultures to look for infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Infection? Could it be related to my transplant or GVHD?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re keeping that in mind, but your symptoms—fever, nausea, and that one loose stool—suggest something like a stomach bug. We’ll rule out bacterial causes first.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your chest X-ray came back. No pneumonia or fluid—just some mild atelectasis at the left base, which is stable. That’s reassuring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not my lungs? I’ve been worried about my BOOP flaring again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No signs of that today. Your oxygen levels are good, and you’re breathing comfortably. We’ll keep monitoring, but this doesn’t look like a lung issue.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your labs show your kidney function is a bit worse—creatinine is 2.2, up from baseline. We’ll watch that closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, that’s not good. I’ve had kidney issues before. Could the fever be hurting my kidneys?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly. Dehydration or infection can affect the kidneys. We’re giving you fluids and will repeat the labs tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re starting you on ciprofloxacin tonight—just in case this is a bacterial gut infection. It covers common enteric bugs.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m already on voriconazole for aspergillosis. Is it safe to add cipro?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good question. Cipro can interact with voriconazole and affect your heart rhythm. So we’re stopping voriconazole for now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will that make my sinus infection come back?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll coordinate with your pulmonologist. You can restart it once you’re off cipro. Your safety comes first.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re also switching your antiviral. You were on famciclovir, but we’re changing to acyclovir—it’s preferred for long-term use after transplant.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that’s fine. I’ve taken acyclovir before. No problem.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: How are you feeling now? Any nausea or chills?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Much better, actually. The chills are gone, and I feel less tired. I even ate a little dinner.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s great to hear. Your body’s likely fighting off whatever caused this. We’ll keep you overnight for observation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my zoster pain? It’s still bothering me, especially at night.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The rash is healed, but nerve pain can linger. Gabapentin is helping, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: A little, but not enough. Could we adjust the dose?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We can increase it tomorrow if needed. For now, let’s focus on getting you stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your blood cultures came back negative—no bacteria growing. That’s a good sign.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not a serious infection?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not a bloodstream one. The stool culture isn’t back yet, but we suspect a mild viral or self-limited bacterial cause.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your repeat labs show your kidney function is stable now, and your white count is normal. You’re doing well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I can go home today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, if you keep feeling this good. We’ll send you home with a five-day course of cipro and the new acyclovir.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And what about the voriconazole?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hold off for now. Call your pulmonologist to restart it after finishing cipro.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Stool culture is back—no salmonella, shigella, or parasites. Everything’s negative. That supports a mild, self-resolving infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m glad it wasn’t anything serious. I’ll watch for fevers and call my oncologist if I feel off again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. You’re strong, Mr. Johnson. This was a bump, but you’ve bounced back quickly. Let’s get your discharge papers ready.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One last thing—your oxygen can stay at home as needed. No changes there.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks, Doctor. I appreciate all the care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take it easy, finish your antibiotics, and follow up with your team.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Nurse will go over your updated medication list, including the new acyclovir and continuing your usual prednisone and CellCept.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. I’ll make sure I have all the prescriptions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re cleared to go home. Call us or your oncologist right away if you develop fever, chills, or feel worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks again for everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care, Mr. Johnson. You’re doing well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just a quick call to confirm—you’re home and feeling okay?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I’m resting, no fever, and ate lunch. Feeling much better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. Keep up the good work. We’ll see you in follow-up as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will do. Appreciate the check-in.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One more thing—your urine protein was a bit high, so your nephrologist may want to adjust your Lasix based on weight.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll monitor my weight like they said.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good plan. Stay hydrated and keep tracking.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Final update: all cultures negative, you’re improving, and no complications. Discharge is confirmed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great. I’m ready to be home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve done well. Just stay alert and call if anything changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Transport is here. Take care, Mr. Johnson.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor. I’ll be in touch if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Mr. Johnson, I'm Dr. Patel. You were brought in today because of fever and weakness. Can you tell me what happened this morning?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I woke up with a bad headache and sore throat. My temperature was 103.2. I threw up twice and just felt too weak to get out of bed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. And you’ve had cough and chills too?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, and rigors—shaking like I was freezing. I haven’t been around anyone sick.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your blood pressure was low when you arrived, and we saw a shadow in your left lung on the chest X-ray. We think you have pneumonia.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Pneumonia? But I’ve been on oxygen at home only when I walk. I didn’t feel short of breath.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Sometimes in patients with your medical history, infections can progress quickly even without classic symptoms. We’ve started IV antibiotics and fluids.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I remember they gave me something for low blood pressure too. I was so dizzy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your blood pressure dropped, likely from dehydration and the infection. We gave you fluids and a steroid called hydrocortisone because you’ve been on prednisone for years—your body might not make enough during stress.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. Last time I was sick, they stopped my voriconazole because of an interaction.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We checked that. Your current antibiotics don’t interact with your usual meds. We’re using vancomycin and ceftazidime to cover all possibilities.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And my kidney numbers? Last time they went up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your creatinine was 2.1, a bit high, but we think it’s from dehydration. It should improve with fluids. We’re monitoring it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I don’t want to end up on dialysis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We don’t expect that. Your labs show no infection in blood, urine, or respiratory viruses. The pneumonia seems isolated.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your chest X-ray yesterday still shows the opacity in your left lung, but your oxygen levels are stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is it getting better?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No significant change yet, but your fever is gone and blood pressure is improving. That’s a good sign the antibiotics are working.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel less tired today. Can I eat?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’re restarting your regular diet. We’ll also switch you back to your home prednisone 3 mg daily instead of IV hydrocortisone.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Another X-ray this morning shows no change in the lung opacity. But clinically, you’re doing better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So why isn’t it clearing?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Infections in immunocompromised patients can take time to resolve on imaging, even when you feel better. We’re not worried.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I’ve been coughing less.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. We’ll keep the IV antibiotics going for now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve developed some diarrhea—up to five loose stools yesterday. We tested it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is it C. diff?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The first two tests were negative, but we’re starting you on metronidazole just in case, since antibiotics can trigger it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Should I stop the antibiotics for pneumonia?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, we need to finish treating the pneumonia. We’ll manage the diarrhea separately.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your diarrhea has improved—only one episode this morning. We’ll continue the metronidazole for now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. And my labs?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Creatinine is down to 1.2, and white count is normal. Your kidneys are recovering.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I go home soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re planning to switch you to oral antibiotics tomorrow—levofloxacin—and if you keep improving, you could go home in a day or two.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re changing your antibiotics to levofloxacin by mouth. You’ve been off IVs since this morning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I’m ready for discharge?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Almost. We want to watch you for one more day on oral meds to make sure you tolerate them and don’t spike a fever.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Makes sense. I’ll take the pills as directed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great news. You’ve had no fever, your cough is nearly gone, and labs are stable. We’re clearing you for discharge tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s wonderful. What about the diarrhea?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Only one loose stool yesterday. We’ll keep you on metronidazole for the full course at home, just to be safe.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the levofloxacin?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll take it for three more days. Total of 14 days from when we started IVs.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll need a note for my oncologist.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, follow-up in one week. Also, the C. diff PCR is still pending, so if diarrhea returns, call your doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. And my other meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Back to your usual regimen—prednisone, Cellcept, carvedilol, and the rest. We’ve updated your list.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I feel much better than when I came in.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve done well. We’ll see you in clinic soon. Get some rest at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your discharge orders are ready. You’re to go home today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great. Just to confirm—I take levofloxacin once daily for three more days?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, and metronidazole every eight hours for the next 13 days. The cough medicine is as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And I restart all my other meds exactly as before?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. And call if you develop fever, worsening cough, or more diarrhea.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you for taking care of me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care, and we’ll see you at your follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just a quick check before you leave. How are you feeling?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Really good. No cough, no fever, and my energy is back.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Excellent. Your lungs are clear on exam, and blood pressure is stable. You’re ready to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m glad this is behind me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Stay hydrated, rest, and take your meds. You’ve come a long way in a week.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care, Mr. Johnson.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One last thing—your wife is here. I’ll go over the discharge instructions with both of you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, please. She helps me keep track of everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Of course. Let’s go over your medications and warning signs one more time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning, Mr. Johnson. I'm Dr. Patel, one of your hospital doctors. I understand you've been feeling quite unwell with nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea for about five days now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, doctor. It started suddenly. I’ve barely been able to keep anything down. I’ve also been feeling dizzy, especially when I stand up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. And you mentioned some cramping in your lower abdomen?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, crampy pain, nothing too severe, but constant. My stool started loose and got watery. No blood though.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And you’ve noticed you’re urinating less than usual?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Definitely. I think that’s why I feel so weak and lightheaded.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. We checked your blood pressure lying down and standing — it drops when you stand, which confirms dehydration. We’re going to start you on IV fluids right away.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that sounds good. I just want to feel more stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Mr. Johnson, your labs came back. Your kidney function is impaired — creatinine is 3.0, which is high for you. Your baseline is around 1.8, correct?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, usually around there. Is this serious?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s concerning, but we believe it’s due to dehydration from the diarrhea and poor intake. Your FeNa is low, which supports that. With IV fluids, we expect it to improve.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not permanent damage?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, this looks like acute kidney injury on top of your chronic kidney disease, and it should reverse as you rehydrate.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank goodness.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We also noticed your liver enzymes are elevated — ALT is 360 and AST is 171. That’s something we need to monitor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My liver? I’ve had issues before with hemochromatosis. Could that be it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly, but we’ve ruled out hepatitis viruses. The timing suggests it could be related to your current infection or possibly graft-versus-host disease. We’ll need to investigate further.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your stool tests came back. It’s negative for C. diff, bacteria, and parasites. But it’s positive for norovirus.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Norovirus? Like the stomach bug? I thought only kids get that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, adults get it too. It’s very contagious. You mentioned your wife had similar symptoms — that fits. It usually resolves on its own, but it hits harder in people like you with weakened immunity.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So that’s what’s causing all this?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, the nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea. We’ll keep supporting you with fluids until it passes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re planning a flexible sigmoidoscopy tomorrow to check your colon. Even though norovirus explains your symptoms, we want to rule out graft-versus-host disease.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that safe? I’m feeling weak.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s a short procedure, and we’ll use minimal sedation. It’s important to check for GVHD, especially with your liver enzymes up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I trust you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The sigmoidoscopy went well. We saw diverticulosis, but the biopsies didn’t show signs of GVHD. The pathologist noted only rare apoptotic cells, not enough to diagnose GVHD.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good news, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, very. And CMV testing was negative, so it’s not that either.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So norovirus is the main culprit?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. But we’re still concerned about your liver. The liver team thinks it could be norovirus affecting the liver directly, or a flare triggered by the infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Do I need a liver biopsy?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not now. You declined, and that’s okay. We’ll monitor your liver enzymes closely as an outpatient. If they don’t improve, we may revisit that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your creatinine is down to 2.1 today — that’s a big improvement from 3.0. Your kidneys are responding well to fluids.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great to hear. And my nausea?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve had no vomiting in over 24 hours. We’re advancing your diet to soft foods today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m actually feeling hungry for the first time in days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your latest labs show creatinine is now 1.7 — back to your baseline. That’s excellent.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the liver?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: ALT and AST are still elevated — around 300. We’ll need to follow up closely. The liver team recommends outpatient monitoring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll do whatever’s needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re stopping allopurinol. It’s not essential, and since your liver is inflamed, we want to reduce any potential burden.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been on that for years. Is it safe to stop?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, especially since your uric acid levels aren’t high. We can restart if needed later.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, makes sense.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re also holding your Bactrim for now. It can affect the liver, and we don’t want to add risk while your enzymes are up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: But I need that for pneumonia prevention, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. We’ll restart it once your liver tests improve. Your oncologist will help coordinate that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve had no diarrhea for two days now. You’re walking well and eating without issues. We’re thinking you could go home tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s wonderful. I’m ready to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll send you home with some lomotil and compazine in case symptoms return. Take them only if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my regular meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, continue all your usual medications except allopurinol and Bactrim — those stay stopped for now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Final update: your creatinine is 1.6, and you’ve had no GI symptoms for over 24 hours. You’re stable for discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great. What about follow-up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll need liver function tests three times this week. Your oncologist and liver clinic will contact you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And if my liver enzymes don’t improve?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Then we may discuss a liver biopsy. But for now, we’re optimistic they’ll trend down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Mr. Johnson, you’re cleared to go home. You look much better — alert, walking, eating well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, doctor. I really appreciate all the care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Remember: take the lomotil or compazine only if symptoms return, and call your doctor if they do.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And I’ll get those liver tests done right away.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Stay hydrated, rest, and we’ll see you in follow-up soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will do. Thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One last thing — your HCV viral load came back negative. So hepatitis C isn’t contributing to your liver issues.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good to know. That was on my mind.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: All right, you’re all set. Take care, Mr. Johnson.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, doctor. I’ll follow up as instructed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just confirming — you understand to restart Bactrim only when your liver tests normalize?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, not until my liver is better. Got it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. And keep taking your prednisone and Cellcept — no changes there.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Those are for my GVHD, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. We didn’t change any of your immunosuppressants.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Nurse will go over your discharge instructions one more time, including your medications and follow-up labs.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll listen carefully.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Final check — any questions before you leave?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, I think I’ve got it all. Thank you for explaining everything so clearly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re very welcome. Take care, and we’ll see you in clinic soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Doctor, one last thing — my cough the other day?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We checked a chest X-ray — no pneumonia. The pulmonary edema from before has resolved. Your cough was likely mild and unrelated.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks. Just wanted to make sure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Of course. All clear.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re officially discharged. Safe travels home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, doctor. I feel much better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Glad to hear it. Take it easy, and call if anything changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello Mr. Johnson, I'm Dr. Patel. I understand you've been having increasing pain around your backside for a few days now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, doctor. It started a few days ago, but since I got home from the last hospital stay, it’s gotten much worse. It’s sharp and tender, especially when I sit.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. You were just discharged from oncology for nausea and diarrhea, correct? Any fever or chills with this pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No fever that I’ve noticed, but my heart’s been racing. I thought it was just from being uncomfortable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. On exam, I felt fullness on the left side near your rectum, and it’s quite tender. We’re concerned this could be a perirectal abscess — a pocket of infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: An abscess? Like an infected cyst? Is that serious?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It can be, especially with your medical history. Because you’ve had a transplant and are on immunosuppressants, infections can spread faster. We recommend draining it right away.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Draining it? Will I need surgery?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, but it’s a minor procedure. You’ll go under anesthesia briefly, we’ll make a small incision to drain the pus, and place a small drain to keep it open so it can continue to drain over the next few days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that sounds reasonable. What happens after?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll start you on IV antibiotics for 24 hours, then switch to oral ones. A nurse will help you care for the drain at home, and you’ll follow up with the surgery clinic in a few days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The procedure went well. We drained a large abscess and placed a Malecot drain. Cultures were taken to check what kind of bacteria are causing the infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. Any idea what caused it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: With your history of chronic diarrhea and immunosuppression, it’s not uncommon. The culture showed Group B Streptococcus and Bacteroides — both can be part of normal gut flora but can cause infection when they get into deeper tissues.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will the antibiotics clear it up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, and because we caught it early and drained it, you should recover well. We’ll keep you on antibiotics and monitor the wound.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news — you’re ready to go home today. The drain is functioning well, and you’re tolerating oral antibiotics.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great. What do I need to do at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll have a visiting nurse come by to help with wound irrigation and drain care. Keep taking the antibiotics, watch for fever or increased pain, and follow up with both surgery and your oncologist.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my other medications — should I restart them?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, all your previous medications should be continued, including prednisone and mycophenolate. We’ve added antibiotics to your list for now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, doctor. I’m glad we caught this in time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take it easy, keep the area clean, and don’t hesitate to call if anything changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The discharge papers are ready. A nurse will go over wound care instructions one more time before you leave.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. I’ll make sure to follow up with my oncologist too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Your complex medical history means close follow-up is key. We’ll coordinate with your team.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Appreciate that. I feel much better already.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello Mr. Johnson, I'm Dr. Patel. I'll be your doctor during this hospital stay. How are you feeling right now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hi, Doctor. I'm a bit tired and short of breath. The cough is really bothering me, and I’ve had diarrhea for a few days now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. You mentioned fevers and chills too. Can you tell me when those started?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: About five days ago. Started with a dry cough, then the fever came, and my muscles started aching. My wife and son got sick too, after me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Thanks for that. We’ve reviewed your history — you’ve had AML, a cord blood transplant, and chronic GVHD. You're on several medications, including prednisone and CellCept.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that’s right. I take them every day. I’ve also had kidney issues for years — my baseline creatinine is around 1.8.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Today your creatinine is 3.1, which is higher than usual. That suggests your kidneys are under stress, likely from dehydration due to the diarrhea and poor intake.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, that makes sense. I haven’t been eating much — I’ve been trying a strict gluten-free, low-potassium diet, but it’s hard to keep food down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll help you stay hydrated with IV fluids. Your sodium is also low — 130 — which fits with the dehydration picture.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that dangerous? The low sodium?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It can be if it drops further, but we’re monitoring it closely. With fluids, it should improve. Now, your cough and low oxygen — we did a chest X-ray.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What did it show?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: There’s a diffuse pattern in your lungs — small nodules and interstitial prominence. It could be viral or an atypical infection. Given your immune status, we want to be cautious.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Could it be pneumonia?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly. We’re starting you on levofloxacin, an antibiotic that covers atypical bacteria, just in case. But your respiratory viral test came back positive.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: For what?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Parainfluenza type 3. It’s a virus that can cause respiratory infections, especially in people with weakened immunity.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh. Is that what my family has too?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Very likely. It spreads easily. The good news is, there’s no sign of bacterial infection in your blood or urine, and your C. diff test was negative.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. What about my heart? I’ve had heart issues before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We checked — your heart sounds normal, no fluid overload. Your ejection fraction has improved since before, so we don’t think this is a heart failure flare-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I was worried about that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning, Mr. Johnson. I’m here to update you. Your second chest X-ray shows the lung opacities have worsened slightly, but still consistent with viral or atypical infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that bad? Is it getting worse?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s not unexpected with parainfluenza. But you’re not getting sicker — your oxygen levels are stable, and you’re breathing comfortably. We’ll keep you on the antibiotic as a precaution.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. What about my diarrhea? It’s still happening.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We tested your stool — no C. diff, no Salmonella, no viruses. Given you’re years past transplant, GVHD is unlikely. It’s probably part of the viral illness.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So no treatment needed?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not specifically. We’ll focus on hydration and nutrition. The diarrhea should resolve as you recover from the virus.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. And my liver tests are up a bit — should I worry?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your ALT and AST are mildly elevated. That’s common in your case — could be from chronic GVHD or iron overload. Nothing acute we need to treat now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news, Mr. Johnson. Your labs today show your kidney function is improving — creatinine down to 2.1. Sodium is normal now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great! Does that mean I can go home soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re planning for discharge tomorrow. Your cough is better, you’re off oxygen, and you’re tolerating food.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m glad. What about my meds? I noticed I’m not getting acyclovir.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good observation. We held acyclovir because it’s cleared by the kidneys, and with your kidney function down, we didn’t want to risk toxicity.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Should I restart it at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hold off for now. Please discuss it with your oncologist at your follow-up. We’ve also added levofloxacin for three more days to finish the course.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Any other changes?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No. All your other meds — prednisone, CellCept, carvedilol, pantoprazole — are continuing as before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Mr. Johnson, you’re cleared to go home today. You look much better — alert, breathing well, and labs are improving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. What should I watch for?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Keep drinking fluids. Weigh yourself every morning — call if you gain more than three pounds, as that could mean fluid retention.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. Any fever or cough return?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, if fever comes back, or you feel short of breath, please call or go to the ER. Also, keep your follow-up with your oncologist — they’ll check your creatinine.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I have an appointment next week. Will I need more antibiotics after today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, this will be the last dose. The levofloxacin was just to cover any bacterial component, but we believe it was mostly viral.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my diarrhea?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Should continue improving. If it persists, let your doctor know — but it’s likely part of the recovery.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor. I really appreciate your care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You're very welcome. Get some rest, stay hydrated, and take care. We’re glad you’re on the mend.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Mr. Johnson, I'm Dr. Patel. You're here because of nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea that started over two weeks ago. How are you feeling right now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Not great. I’ve been so weak and achy. I can’t keep anything down, and I’ve had loose stools the whole time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. Your labs show your kidney function is worse than usual—creatinine is 4.4, which is high for you. We think it’s from dehydration due to poor intake and diarrhea. We’re starting IV fluids to help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, that makes sense. My last admission was similar. But I also have this nagging cough now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we noticed. Your chest X-ray shows some changes at the base of your right lung. It could be atelectasis or early pneumonia. We’ll keep an eye on it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Should we be worried about infection? I’m immunocompromised.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. That’s why we’re being thorough. We sent stool tests to check for infections like C. diff, viruses, and parasites.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—your stool test came back negative for C. diff, Salmonella, Shigella, and parasites. But we did find adenovirus.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Adenovirus? Isn’t that just a cold virus?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It can cause respiratory illness, but in transplant patients like you, it can also cause severe gastrointestinal infection. That’s likely why you’ve been so sick.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is it dangerous?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It can be, but we have a treatment—cidofovir. We’ll give one dose, and it should clear the virus. We’ll also give IVIG to boost your immunity.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve placed a PICC line so we can give you medications and nutrition safely over the next few days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I’ve had one before. Will I need IV nutrition?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, for now. You’re not tolerating food, and we need to make sure you get proper nutrition while your gut heals.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We did an EGD and colonoscopy today to check for GVHD or other causes. Biopsies show no GVHD—just mild gastritis. That’s reassuring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s really just the adenovirus?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. And we gave cidofovir yesterday. Your adenovirus levels are already dropping. That’s a great sign.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your kidney function improved with fluids, but now it’s rising again. We’re concerned about acute tubular necrosis. We’ll adjust your meds and monitor closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that serious?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It is, but it’s often reversible. We’ll avoid nephrotoxic drugs and keep you well-hydrated. Your nephrologist is on board.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve developed redness and swelling near your old perirectal abscess scar. An ultrasound shows a new fluid collection. It’s likely a recurrent abscess.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh no. Will I need surgery?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, the surgeons will drain it tomorrow. We’ll start antibiotics to cover skin and gut bacteria.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The abscess was successfully drained. Cultures grew mixed flora and Bacteroides. You’re on daptomycin and Zosyn, dosed for your kidney function.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m glad that’s done. But my cough is getting worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your oxygen levels are dropping. A CT scan shows pneumonia in your upper lobes, likely atypical. We’re starting meropenem and voriconazole just in case it’s fungal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: But the adenovirus is gone, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, but your immune system is still weak. You’re vulnerable to other infections. We’re being aggressive to prevent complications.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You spiked a fever last night. We’re broadening antibiotics and watching your breathing closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Mr. Johnson, you just had a severe coughing fit and vomited. Your oxygen dropped suddenly. We need to intubate you and move you to the ICU.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I can’t breathe… okay, do what you need.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re in the ICU. You were intubated last night due to respiratory failure. A chest X-ray shows pulmonary edema. We’re giving diuretics to remove fluid.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not just pneumonia?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No. Your heart function is reduced, and the stress of infection caused fluid buildup in your lungs. We’re treating it with Lasix and close monitoring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We did a bronchoscopy. Cultures came back negative—no bacteria, virus, or fungus. That’s surprising but good. It means your body may be clearing the infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So can we stop antibiotics?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll taper them soon. For now, we’re finishing the course. We also stopped voriconazole—fungal markers were negative.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great news—you’re off the ventilator and breathing on your own. Your lungs are clearing, and your oxygen levels are stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I can breathe easier. When can I eat?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll start with small sips and advance slowly. You’ve been on TPN, but we’ll transition to oral intake as you tolerate.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your hemoglobin is low—7.2. It’s been dropping. We’re checking for causes like parvovirus or bone marrow issues.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Do I need a transfusion?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not yet. We’re monitoring. We’d like to do a bone marrow biopsy, but I understand you’re hesitant.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’d rather avoid it if possible.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We respect that. We’ll repeat labs at follow-up. If it’s still low, we may need to reconsider.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your HHV-6 level peaked at 992 but is now decreasing. We didn’t treat it, but we’ll keep monitoring as an outpatient.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that dangerous?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It can be in transplant patients, but you’re not showing symptoms. We’ll watch it closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your creatinine is now 3.3 and stable. Kidney function is improving. We’ll keep you on Lasix for heart failure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been weighing myself daily. No big changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. That’s key for heart failure. Call if you gain more than 3 pounds in a day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. We’re planning discharge in a few days. You’ll go home with services and a walker for support.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m ready to go home. What meds will I be on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll continue carvedilol, aspirin, and prednisone. We’re adding Lasix 80mg daily for heart failure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re stopping CellCept—it increases infection risk. Bactrim is now once daily for easier dosing. You’ll also take fluconazole for fungal prevention.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the nebulizer?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, ipratropium for cough. Use it every 4 hours as needed. A machine will be sent to your home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your labs are stable. Hemoglobin is still low, but we’ll follow up with oncology. Zinc and vitamin D levels are improving with supplements.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll finish the zinc course and recheck levels.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. And keep taking the multivitamin. Your ferritin is very high—over 6,500—so we’ll discuss iron chelation with your team.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Today’s the day. You’re being discharged. You’ve made incredible progress—through adenovirus, abscess, pneumonia, and respiratory failure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I couldn’t have done it without you all. Thank you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re strong. Remember: take Lasix daily, weigh yourself, and call if you gain weight or feel short of breath.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Follow up with cardiology, nephrology, and oncology. Get your CBC and Chem-7 labs done this week and fax them to your doctors.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll do that. And I’ll use the nebulizer as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. You’re going home with a commode and nursing support. Take it slow, and call us with any concerns.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks again, Doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care, Mr. Johnson.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: One more thing—my HHV-6 level is pending. Should I worry?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No need to worry now. We’ll check it at follow-up. If it rises, we’ll discuss treatment.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that helps. I feel ready to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve earned it. We’ll be here if you need us.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I appreciate that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Discharge papers are ready. Nurse will go over everything one more time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great. I’ll review them carefully.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve been through a lot, but you’re on the mend. Keep up the good work.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you for everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Our pleasure. Take care and stay well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. See you at follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Looking forward to it. Have a safe trip home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re very welcome. Rest well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I plan to.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take it easy. We’re here if you need us.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello Mr. Johnson, I'm Dr. Patel. I'll be your doctor during this stay. You were admitted for diarrhea and vomiting. Can you tell me more about what’s been going on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hi, yes. I’ve had six watery bowel movements last night, and two episodes of yellow vomit. No blood in the toilet, but I saw some on the tissue. I feel weak and thirsty.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. Any abdominal pain, fever, or dizziness?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, no pain or fever. I’m not lightheaded. But I’ve lost about 30 pounds in the last six weeks. My appetite’s been poor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s significant. You mentioned your son’s family was sick recently?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, a few of them had vomiting starting four days ago. We spent time together last week.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That helps. Given your history, especially the recent adenovirus infection, we’re concerned about another gastrointestinal infection. We’ll run some tests.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Could it be adenovirus again? I was just treated for that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s possible. We’ve sent a PCR test for adenovirus, but results will take a few days. In the meantime, we’re treating you for dehydration with IV fluids.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. My kidneys have been bad before—could this affect them?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your creatinine was elevated at 4.0, which is higher than your baseline of around 2.0–2.5. This is likely due to dehydration from vomiting and diarrhea. We expect it to improve with fluids.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my heart? I’ve had fluid issues before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good question. Your chest X-ray shows stable heart size, no new fluid in the lungs. We’ve held your Lasix for now to avoid over-diuresis while you're dehydrated.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Makes sense. I’ve been on prednisone and CellCept for GVHD—CellCept was stopped recently.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’re continuing your low-dose prednisone, Bactrim, and valacyclovir. GVHD is less likely since you’re improving without steroid escalation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve also had some neck pain and burning when I pee lately.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We checked your urine—it shows no infection. The neck pain isn’t associated with stiffness or light sensitivity, so we don’t suspect meningitis. We’ll keep an eye on it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your stool tests came back—no C. diff, no salmonella, shigella, or parasites. Norovirus is negative too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So not C. diff again? That’s good, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that’s good. It means we don’t need antibiotics. We still suspect a viral infection, possibly adenovirus. Your kidney function is already improving—creatinine down to 3.4.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. Can I eat anything yet?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re starting you on a low-residue, lactose-free diet. Small meals first—let’s see how you tolerate it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your creatinine is now 2.7, and potassium has normalized. You’re doing well. We’re going to restart Lasix at a lower dose—40 mg instead of 60 mg.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Why lower it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Because your weight is down to 214.9 pounds from 217.6, and we don’t want to over-diurese. We’re balancing heart and kidney function.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. Any update on the adenovirus test?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Still pending. But since your symptoms are resolving without specific antiviral treatment, it may not change management.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve had no diarrhea for two days, and labs continue to improve. We’re confident you’re on the mend.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. I feel stronger. Can I go home soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re planning for discharge tomorrow if all goes well. You’ll go home with services—someone to check in on you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I’ll need help with meals and meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: All set for discharge today. Your adenovirus PCR is still pending, but we’ll follow up with you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my Lasix? I’m on 40 mg now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, 40 mg daily. We’ll adjust if needed. Weigh yourself every morning—call if you gain more than three pounds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. What about the small bump on my arm where the IV was?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s a small fluid collection—likely from the IV. It’s mildly tender but not infected. It should resolve on its own.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And my other meds—same as before?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, same doses: prednisone, Bactrim, valacyclovir, pantoprazole, metoprolol, and the others. Continue all as prescribed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been depressed lately—still on escitalopram?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, and we encourage you to follow up with your mental health provider. Don’t stop it suddenly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I won’t. Any restrictions?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Avoid heavy lifting. Use your walker as needed. Stay hydrated, but don’t overdo fluids. Watch for nausea, fever, or swelling.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And when do I see my oncologist?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your follow-up is scheduled in five days. They’ll review the adenovirus and HHV-6 results when they come back.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: HHV-6? Was that tested?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, sent during this admission. It was checked due to your immunocompromised state, but results are still pending.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I’ll keep an eye on things and call if anything changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. You’re doing well. We’re discharging you home with services. A nurse will call tomorrow to check in.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor. I appreciate all the care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care, and we’ll see you soon in follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just a quick call to check in—how are you feeling at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Much better. No diarrhea, eating well, and I’ve been weighing myself daily.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Excellent. Keep it up. We’ll get your test results soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Final update: your adenovirus PCR and HHV-6 results are still pending, but given your recovery, they won’t change your care plan.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Understood. I’ll follow up with my team.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, they’ll have the results soon. Continue all medications and monitoring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will do. Thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care, Mr. Johnson.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just confirming your discharge is official as of today. You’ve completed your admission successfully.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. I’m home and doing well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. Stay in touch with your care team.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you for everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You're very welcome. Get some rest.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I plan to.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Have a good recovery.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks, Doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello Mr. Johnson, I'm Dr. Patel. I understand you've been feeling worse over the past few days. Can you tell me what brought you in today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, doctor. I’ve been short of breath, especially when I lie down. And my cough has gotten worse—now it’s bringing up phlegm.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. And how many words can you speak before needing to stop for breath?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Maybe four or five. It’s been really hard to talk. My wife noticed I was wheezing too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s significant. Your oxygen level at home was 79%, which is quite low. We did a chest X-ray when you arrived.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is it my heart again? I was off my water pill because my kidneys were acting up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, the X-ray shows signs of fluid in your lungs—pulmonary edema—consistent with a heart failure flare-up. But there’s also a patch in your right lung that looks like pneumonia.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh no. I’ve had pneumonia before. That was scary.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re concerned about a type called HCAP—healthcare-associated pneumonia—so we started you on strong antibiotics: levofloxacin and cefepime.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And what about the fluid? I thought I got a diuretic in the ER.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You did—40 mg of IV Lasix. But you’ve only passed a little urine so far. We’re going to give you more—80 mg IV twice a day—to help your body get rid of the extra fluid.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: But my kidneys… they’ve been bad before. Is that safe?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re watching closely. Your creatinine is 3.3, which is high, but we need to balance heart and kidney function. We’ll check your labs daily.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my potassium was high last time. That’s dangerous, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it was 7.5 on admission—very high. But we gave you treatment to bring it down, and it’s now 4.9. We’ll keep monitoring it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I don’t want another emergency like last time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your second dose of Lasix helped. The repeat chest X-ray shows improvement in lung congestion.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. I do feel a bit easier breathing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We also tested for viruses and infections. Your respiratory viral panel was negative—no flu, RSV, or adenovirus.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s bacterial pneumonia?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Likely. We also checked for Legionella and cryptococcus—both negative. Blood cultures are pending.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my heart? Is the damage from chemo still the cause?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We think your weak heart function—25% ejection fraction—is due to either chemotherapy or GVHD. But right now, we’re focused on treating the flare-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your third X-ray shows continued improvement. The fluid is decreasing, and the pneumonia area is clearing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. Can I stop the IV meds soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re switching your antibiotics to oral levofloxacin. You’ll finish the full course before discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the Lasix? I’m peeing more now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, but your creatinine went up to 3.7, so we’re pausing IV Lasix today to protect your kidneys.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I’m stuck between heart and kidneys again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re balancing both. You’ve lost weight—from 222.6 to 219 pounds—so the fluid is coming off. We’ll reassess tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The latest X-ray shows your lungs are much clearer. No more overt edema. Just a small remaining effusion.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my breathing?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re speaking in full sentences now. That’s a big improvement. Your oxygen is 100% on room air.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I go home soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly by tomorrow. We’ll finish your antibiotic course, and your labs look stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
